title: The Money Pit of Oak Island

pages.text: Mr Dankwa wrote on the board: 1795. “In that year, in Canada, a sixteen-year-old boy named Daniel McGinnis walked on a small island called Oak Island. He found a dip in the ground near a big oak tree. What would you do?” “Dig!” shouted Baba.
sentences: Mr Dankwa wrote on the board: 1795.
“In that year, in Canada, a sixteen-year-old boy named Daniel McGinnis walked on a small island called Oak Island.
He found a dip in the ground near a big oak tree.
What would you do?” “Dig!” shouted Baba.
pages.alt: A teacher points to a date on the board while a class looks at a map of an island.

pages.text: Daniel and two friends did. They found a filled-in shaft and kept digging. At about 9 metres, they stopped. Later, in 1804, a team reached around 30 metres. Then salt water flooded the shaft. “Where did the water come from?” asked Emefa. “Good question,” said Mr Dankwa.
sentences: Daniel and two friends did.
They found a filled-in shaft and kept digging.
At about 9 metres, they stopped.
Later, in 1804, a team reached around 30 metres.
Then salt water flooded the shaft.
“Where did the water come from?” asked Emefa.
“Good question,” said Mr Dankwa.
pages.alt: Boys dig a deep shaft in 1795 while water begins to seep in.

pages.text: “Later diggers found tunnels that seemed to link the pit to the sea,” said Mr Dankwa. “Some say they were built to flood the pit and protect treasure. Others say nature could have made the tunnels, or the pit may be a sinkhole.” Emefa wrote both ideas down.
sentences: “Later diggers found tunnels that seemed to link the pit to the sea,” said Mr Dankwa.
“Some say they were built to flood the pit and protect treasure.
Others say nature could have made the tunnels, or the pit may be a sinkhole.” Emefa wrote both ideas down.
pages.alt: A diagram shows a pit connected by tunnels to the sea.

pages.text: “What treasure?” asked Baba. “Stories say pirates like Captain Kidd, or even Inca refugees, buried it,” said Mr Dankwa. “But notice: those are stories. Over more than two hundred years, with a great deal of money spent, nobody has found treasure.”
sentences: “What treasure?” asked Baba.
“Stories say pirates like Captain Kidd, or even Inca refugees, buried it,” said Mr Dankwa.
“But notice: those are stories.
Over more than two hundred years, with a great deal of money spent, nobody has found treasure.”
pages.alt: Pirate and treasure-chest drawings are crossed out with a question mark.

pages.text: “In 1971, a camera was lowered about 60 metres down,” said Mr Dankwa. “Some people think the blurry pictures show chests. Others are not sure. Blurry is not proof.” Emefa underlined the word proof.
sentences: “In 1971, a camera was lowered about 60 metres down,” said Mr Dankwa.
“Some people think the blurry pictures show chests.
Others are not sure.
Blurry is not proof.” Emefa underlined the word proof.
pages.alt: A grainy underwater camera image on a screen with a question mark.

pages.text: “Digging there has also been dangerous,” said Mr Dankwa. “Four treasure hunters died in a single accident in 1965. The island is covered in holes.” “So why do they keep going?” asked Baba. “Hope is powerful,” said Mr Dankwa. “And a mystery that is never answered is hard to stop wondering about.”
sentences: “Digging there has also been dangerous,” said Mr Dankwa.
“Four treasure hunters died in a single accident in 1965.
The island is covered in holes.” “So why do they keep going?” asked Baba.
“Hope is powerful,” said Mr Dankwa.
“And a mystery that is never answered is hard to stop wondering about.”
pages.alt: A hole-pocked island with warning signs.

pages.text: Emefa made a chart. Known: the pit is real, and digging flooded it. Not known: who made the pit, how, and whether any treasure was ever there. “A good detective,” she said, “asks: what evidence would change my mind?” Baba grinned. “A chest of gold,” he said.
sentences: Emefa made a chart.
Known: the pit is real, and digging flooded it.
Not known: who made the pit, how, and whether any treasure was ever there.
“A good detective,” she said, “asks: what evidence would change my mind?” Baba grinned.
“A chest of gold,” he said.
pages.alt: A student makes a chart of Known and Not known for the pit.

pages.text: At the end, Mr Dankwa wrote one rule: Never dig deep holes, especially near the sea. “It is dangerous,” he said. “A real mystery must be investigated safely, by trained people.” Emefa closed her notebook. “So it is a mystery because we have a hole and a story,” she said, “but no proof of the treasure.” “Exactly,” he said. The end.

activities.question: What stopped the diggers going deeper in 1804?

activities.prompt: After more than 200 years of digging, what do you think the evidence shows about the treasure?

activities.question: Why did Mr Dankwa say “blurry is not proof”?
options: A blurry picture cannot show for sure what is down there

activities.definition: A deep, narrow hole dug into the ground.

activities.prompt: Put the story of the pit in order.
items: In 1795, Daniel McGinnis found a dip in the ground.
Diggers reached about 9 metres and later about 30 metres.

activities.prompt: People kept digging because of hope. When is hope helpful, and when can it lead us to take risks?

glossary.definition: A deep, narrow hole dug into the ground.
A hole that forms when the ground collapses.
Evidence that shows something is true.
A store of valuable things such as gold or jewels.
